new_statements.quote: A main word stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words. [p. 560] ... In non-final syllables the preferred pattern is more often vv, very possibly under the influence of a new tendency towards antepenultimate word stress: CVV-CVv#. [p. 560] ... Mekeo is a stress-timed language oriented to a system of predetermined word stresses (with the main stress on the penultimate syllable and a secondary stress on every second syllable leftward from that). [p. 67] ... Normal word stress in Mekeo falls on the penultimate syllable of the word - as happens here with perfective aspect (which is thus unmarked). [p. 249]
new_statements.citation: Jones, Alan A. 1998. Towards a lexicogrammar of Mekeo (an Austronesian language of West Central Papua). Pacific Linguistics C-138. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, ANU.
new_statements.locator: Appendix 1 'Essentials of Mekeo phonology', section C 'Phonotactics and morphophonemics', p. 560 (PDF p. 580); supporting statements §1.3.3.3 p. 67 (PDF p. 87) and §4.2.1 p. 249 (PDF p. 269)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words in all four dialects; secondary stresses fall on alternate syllables leftward from the penult. Departures from the default are grammatical (marked): intransitive verbs shift stress forward onto the subject-marking prefix to signal imperfective aspect (e-mai 'has come' vs. é-mai 'is coming'), and some words carry marked final stress reflecting an assimilated 3SG suffix (EMek feló 'good') or object-marking suffixes; Jones also notes an incipient tendency toward antepenultimate stress in words with a final diphthong.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on every second syllable leftward from the penult (p. 67); in verb phrases adverbial co-verbs and some suffixes shift the main stress and leave secondary stress on the root.
new_statements.exceptions: Marked/fronted stress on the subject marker of intransitive verbs signals imperfective aspect (pp. 249, 234); marked final stress in EMek felo 'good' and in forms with assimilated 3SG suffix -a / 'compensatory' stress (pp. 124, 310, 494); suffix -n-i-a moves main stress rightward to the last root syllable and -mo makes stress fall on a new penult (p. 502); reduplicated forms may have a single main stress on the antepenult (poapoa 'tattoo', ugauga 'sorcerer', p. 218); the particle MO is stressed or unstressed with different functions; a 'new tendency towards antepenultimate word stress' in CVV-CVv# words (p. 560).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress (polysyllabic words, all four dialects, pandialectal description); Jones also describes phrase-level tonic prominence (pitch accent on the focus) separately in §1.3.3.3. Vowel length is stated to be phonemic (p. 560), but Blust 2013 reports Jones as saying it is not contrastive; not relevant to stress placement.
new_statements.identity_note: Jones 1998 is an explicitly pandialectal description covering all four Mekeo dialects — East Mekeo (the mission 'standard', Veifa'a), West Mekeo, North Mekeo (Amoamo) and North-West Mekeo (Kovio) — plus the Papangongo and Engefa communalects; the penultimate-stress statement in Appendix 1 is stated for the language as a whole, with most examples in EMek. All fall under glottocode meke1243 (Mekeo, alt. Kovio/Mekeo-Kovio). Jones notes that the Papangongo communalect differs from West Mekeo 'mainly by word-stress patterns more typical of EMek' (p. 20).

sources.note: Appendix 1 'Essentials of Mekeo phonology', §C, p. 560: 'A main word stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words'; notes 'a new tendency towards antepenultimate word stress: CVV-CVv#'. §1.3.3.3 p. 67: stress-timed, main stress penultimate, secondary stress on every second syllable leftward. §4.2.1 p. 249: 'Normal word stress in Mekeo falls on the penultimate syllable of the word'; intransitive verbs take marked fronted stress on the subject prefix for imperfective aspect; some forms (EMek felo 'good', 3SG-suffixed words) carry marked final ('compensatory') stress.

sources.citation: Jones, Alan Anthony. 1993. Towards a lexicogrammar of Mekeo. PhD thesis, Australian National University. Handle 1885/133193.
sources.note: Same statements as the 1998 book (thesis version): 'A main word stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words'; 'Mekeo is a stress-timed language... main stress on the penultimate syllable and a secondary stress on every second syllable leftward'; 'Normal word stress in Mekeo falls on the penultimate syllable of the word'; fronted stress on subject marker = imperfective.

sources.citation: Strong, W. M. 1913-14. The Roro and Mekeo languages of British New Guinea. Zeitschrift für Kolonialsprachen 4: 285-311.
sources.note: Gives an 'Accent' rule for RORO only (p. 286: two syllables - first; three syllables - first if it contains a diphthong, otherwise second; longer words - second syllable). The Mekeo 'Phonetics' section (p. 303) discusses the guttural k, ng and a vowel 'break' but says nothing about accent/stress in Mekeo.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2013. The Austronesian languages (rev. ed.). Asia-Pacific Linguistics. (ch. 4 Sound systems, pp. 198-199 on Mekeo).
sources.note: Discusses Mekeo consonant inventories (Pawley 1975, Ross 1988, Jones 1998) and absence of contrastive vowel length; no statement on Mekeo stress.
